Port St Johns

By: Stenette Grosskopf | Delivery

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
One way or another the community of Port St Johns is fighting to save their town!

Unique Selling Point:
Port St Johns on the SA Wild Coast falls under the OR Thambo Municipality. The local community is sick and tired of the town being mismanaged and have taken matters into their own hands. The Tourism Foundation has embarked on an aggressive "town beautification" project, new investment is earmarked for the town, and now municipal workers have started protesting, saying enough is enough! Municipal workers say they were promised an increase on 30 October 2017. MEC for Cooperate Governance and Traditional Affairs, Fikile Xasa was called upon to find a solution, but instead he sent someone from his office to deal with the matter. This angered the workers who to date have still not received their increases. At first they stopped collecting municipal waste, and when the mayor and councillors refused to remedy the situation they decided to dump all the town's rubbish on and in town hall and at the municipal's offices. They have also resorted to defacing the Town Hall with faeces.

Summary:
The Mayor of Port St Johns, Ms Lindelwa Rolobile, promised salary increases to municipal workers in October last year. However, nothing has come of it. Now workers are angry about the lack of action and last week they dumped a truckload of the town's waste in and around the Town Hall and municipal offices. While the Port St Johns Tourism Forum have been hard at work to try and raise the town's profile and put it back on the tourism map, their plans could now be derailed by negative publicity of filth and waste on the streets of Port St Johns.

In the meantime the Mayor and councillors of Port St Johns have been ordered to embark on a cleanup operation at their own cost. Source of order is being traced but comes from within the ANC.

Further information:
Last week it was also reported that the small town of Port St Johns on the Wild Coast in the Eastern Cape is set for a facelift with plans for a state-of-the-art R100m holiday resort. The Mangrove Place is spearheaded by local developer EuroblitzPolela Consortium. The plan is for locals to be trained as bricklayers, electricians, plumbers and carpenters, to be used in the building of the resort, and as an upliftment programme for the impoverished community. However, it seems the mayor is willing to put this and other efforts by the Tourism Forum at risk by failing to engage with the angry mob of municipal workers.

In an effort to put the town back on the tourism map, the local Tourism Forum has started "colouring in the town", making it a true rainbow town. Road shoulders are painted in vibrant colours, along with many other public fixtures like park benches, dustbins and shopfronts. Making for bright vibrant visuals in contrast with the state of the Town Hall.

Press Release:


Port St Johns
Tired of municipal mismanagement, the community of Port St Johns has decided to take matters into its own hands. The town’s Tourism Foundation has embarked on an aggressive beautification project through cleaning and painting infrastructure like bridges and sidewalks. Carte Blanche takes a tour of the town


Script:


Port St Johns
Kids Singing...

OPENING LINK
It's one of the most scenic places in the country and it's been a popular holiday destination for many decades, but it's a very different picture when you get into the actual town of Port St Johns a couple of kms down the road.
V/o
The town is nestled against the mouth of the Umzimvubu river on the Eastern Cape wild coast. Like ants, people scurry along, in and out the local shops, amenities and taxis.
V/o
As with so many other small towns across South Africa, Port St Johns has had its fair share of service delivery problems. Unemployment is rife and life is hard for most people here.
Steve UPSOUND
Derek: Your business you say is still going?

Steve: Ja, it's going it's going although things are bad but I'm trying to push.

Derek: Times are tight.
V/o
Everywhere you go you see the signs of the most recent municipal workers' strike. For almost 4 months no-one was cleaning the town and by December they were literally knee-deep in rubbish.
Amanda
It was in season and I was having to explain to every guest who didn't turn away – because a lot of them did – I'm really sorry it's a Union/Municipal and community struggle and we apologise for this and and every guest was like “oh my god this is disgusting”.
V/o
Amanda Weerdenburg is a business owner and part of the local Port St Johns Tourism Forum.
Amanda
And you had to in order to save your reputation, go to every client and then sit there for the 20 minutes and not politically have a side and listen to their upset experience of the town. A lot of them were like “we're not coming back”. Word of mouth it just spread. So we lost a lot of business.
V/o
The continued strike and unsanitary conditions in town were affecting everyone.
BOY
I really feel disappointed in our people because when they are dirtying the streets it is them again that's going to clean it.
Vanessa
The whole town was stinking, and you know if was actually sad to see our children walking in filth so I tried as much to advise the children not to go into the town central.
V/o
Desperate to save their town, and to counter a wave of negative publicity on social media the town's Tourism Forum came up with a plan.
LINK
There's absolutely nothing new about a small town battling with the municipality and a dire lack of service delivery. But here in Port St Johns the community is rising up, not with threats or violence, but with paintbrushes.
Amanda
So we decided to create a solution for ourselves that involved the town. There has been some youtube clips and stuff about slums and disadvantaged areas across the world and how colour sort of just uplifted people's spirits. Then they got involved.

Derek: Like in India?

Ja, in India and Indonesia as well. So we created a competition so that the community need to either paint a door or a pole and we would try and get some donations.And then we went to the whatsapp group and said right, we're going. Everybody who wants to paint, lets do it on the weekends because we're all busy and we started to paint the bridges.
Monica
And we started painting. And we started painting. And then 2 securities from the municipality came and then these guys came and say “who gave you permission to paint the bridge?” I'm like excuse me sir I thin you're supposed to be watching the municipality because we're very busy, or else grab a paint brush...
V/o
Monical Small is also part of the Tourism Forum and has been one of the driving forces behind the painting project.
Monica
We're doing it for fun and just to up the moral of the people because I mean when all of this was going on none of us were happy. But it's brought some brightness because even the municipal workers they were coming into town and obviously sitting around But they were looking around and seeing brightness. And they actually moved to come and sit here because they were sitting under the trees. So when this was painted and looking nice they came and they sat here so at least it is boosting some people. I mean, I've literally seen people taking selfies on the bridge. That never happened before. So, ja... that's nice.
V/o
What started as two women painting a bridge, has expanded to people from all walks of life taking up paint brushes, and helping to bring colour to the town.
Victoria
Okay, she says she's very proud of the painting because it just brightened up the town and even though they were dirtying the town they saw what we were doing and they liked it that's why even when they were throwing the extra dirt they didn't go and throw on the bridges.
V/o
Victoria is one of the colorful locals of the town and has been actively involved in the project from early on.
Monica
She was our traffic person because whenever the people come and say they are looking for jobs she says no this is your bridge grab a brush. And even when the people are walking she says no you're going to dirty this. She's our sort of mascot of town because she's very vocal about anything.
LINK
It's not just the older members of the community getting involved. Here at Nobuhle Primary School there's a passion from the young learners to paint and get involved in uplifting the town.
Vanessa
I approached my learners and asked them if they are interested in painting and they wanted to paint immediately. So they are very enthusiastic about it and they can't wait to do the next project.
V/o
The school is on the hill overlooking the town, in amongst the typical rural homes dotting the Eastern Cape landscape like hundreds and thousands. If you're one of the lucky few you have a toilet and a water tank to collect rainwater. Otherwise your lot is to carry 20l buckets of water up this hill.
Simpiwe
You can't make anything with a 20l bucket because you have to use water in houses so 20l can't make anything but the distance is killing you. You can't even make the...

DEREK: It's a long way to drive never-mind carry 20l of water.

Yes you can't even do the laundry and anything that you have to do.
V/o
Simphiwe has lived in Port St Johns for most his life and like most of the locals he is unemployed and struggles to make a living.
Simpiwe
DEREK: You grew up here?

I grew up here. This is my room, this one. This is my aunty's room who are using it, and also this is my brother's room there at the back. I am strying here. That's where I grew up to.
V/o
During December he helped out at one of the holiday resorts, but if there are no tourists, there is no work.
Amanda
The future of South Africa's youth have to get involved into tourism because it's a key consistent factor. And for a town like this we need to have the tourists confidence to come back. And the future of these children, need to understand that tourism isn't just about selling a bed, from getting off the plane to leaving the plane. So South Africa needs to have a positive “#wedotoursim”-energy, and that involves everybody from the bus driver tot he kids selling their little clay cars on the side of the streets.
Vanessa
Port St Johns was known as paradise and now we are actually with this painting we are actually trying to bring back the garden of eden.
V/o
Of course there are those who are not keen on the painting that say the residents are simply treating the symptoms of something much bigger
Amanda
Derek: But do some people say that it's just a plaster over a sore.

Yeah, probably. And they're probably right in a way. But what would you do? If you were living in knee deep and the politics were crazy and there was threats everywhere. What would you do? Would you run away? Or would you try and find a solution?

Derek: I would pick up my paintbrush.

There you go.


PROMO 10”
In Port St Johns on the Eastern Cape wild coast the local community is coming together to find a way of putting the town back on the tourism map.


PROMO 15”
The residents of Port St Johns is teaching the rest of South Africa the true meaning of “Rainbow Nation”.

Amanda: If you were living in knee deep and the politics were crazy and there was threats everywhere. What would you do? Would you run away? Or would you try and find a solution?


PROMO 15”
UPSOUND I really feel disappointed in our people because when they are dirtying the streets it is them again that's going to clean it.

For the past 4 months Port St Johns has been drowning in waste, but the community is rising up and is determined to turn the tide.
